title: Module 1 Gate Quiz
description:
Take this quiz after you finish the Module 1 interactive walkthrough. It has 10 questions, one attempt, a 30-minute limit, and is closed-AI (calculator and scratch paper only). Enter numeric answers as plain numbers, with no $, commas or % sign. Your numbers are different from other students’ numbers.

  • 8 of 10 (80%) or higher meets the gate. The Mastery Quiz is optional for you.
  • Below 80%: choose one Step 3 option (Remedial Chapter Walkthrough, lecture path, or practice problems) and take the Mastery Quiz.
  • The higher of your Gate Quiz and Mastery Quiz scores counts for the module.

qs.neutral_comments_html: Different users need different information. Lenders, suppliers and bond investors focus on the ability to pay and to survive. Owners and boards focus on return, performance and growth.

Whether Cullowhee has the cash and short-term resources to pay its bills on time
How much Cullowhee earns on the owners’ investment and how fast it can grow

qs.neutral_comments_html: Total assets are financed by liabilities and equity. When liabilities are part of the financing, equity is smaller than total assets, so the same net income gives a higher return on equity than on assets.
qs.question_text: In FY2026 Cullowhee’s ROA was 5.7% and its ROE was 10.4%. Which statement best explains why ROE is higher than ROA?

answers.answer_html: Creditors finance part of the assets, so the same income is earned on a smaller base of owners’ equity (financial leverage).
Owners’ equity is larger than total assets.
ROE uses sales in the denominator, which is larger than assets.
ROE includes dividends in the numerator.

qs.neutral_comments_html: FY2025 ROA ≈ 6.5% × 1.34 = 8.7%. FY2026 ROA ≈ 4.9% × 1.16 = 5.7%. Margin fell and turnover fell, so both pushed ROA down.
qs.question_text: Cullowhee’s profit margin was 6.5% in FY2025 and 4.9% in FY2026. Its asset turnover was 1.34 in FY2025 and 1.16 in FY2026. ROA = profit margin × asset turnover. Which statement best explains the change in ROA?

answers.answer_html: ROA rose because asset turnover rose.
ROA did not change because the two measures offset each other.
ROA fell because both profit margin and asset turnover fell.
ROA fell only because profit margin fell; asset turnover rose.

title: Module 1 Mastery Quiz
description:
The Mastery Quiz is a second look at the same ideas with different questions. It is optional if you met the 80% gate on the Gate Quiz, and recommended after a Step 3 option if you did not. It has 10 questions, one attempt, a 30-minute limit, and is closed-AI (calculator and scratch paper only). Enter numeric answers as plain numbers, with no $, commas or % sign.

The higher of your Gate Quiz and Mastery Quiz scores counts for Module 1, so an optional attempt cannot lower your grade.

qs.question_text: In FY2026 Cullowhee’s net income was $2,679 thousand but cash provided by operating activities was $4,564 thousand. Which statement best explains the difference?

answers.answer_html: Depreciation and other noncash expenses were added back, and they were larger than the cash tied up in receivables and inventory.
Net income is reduced by dividends, which are paid from operating cash.
Depreciation is a cash payment, so it increases operating cash flow.
Cash from operations includes the proceeds of the bond issue.

qs.question_text: A growing company reports rising net income but falling cash from operating activities. Which is the most likely explanation?

answers.answer_html: The company paid a cash dividend.
Receivables and inventories grew faster than sales, tying up cash.

qs.question_text: Which one of these requires a month-end adjustment at Cullowhee?

A dealer paid its invoice in full on the last day of the month.
Cullowhee bought a delivery van for cash on the last day of the month.
Cullowhee paid a supplier on the 30th for parts bought last month.

title: Module 3 Mastery Quiz
description:
The Mastery Quiz is a second look at the same ideas with different questions. It is optional if you met the 80% gate on the Gate Quiz, and recommended after a Step 3 option if you did not. It has 10 questions, one attempt, a 30-minute limit, and is closed-AI (calculator and scratch paper only). Enter numeric answers as plain numbers, with no $, commas or % sign.

The higher of your Gate Quiz and Mastery Quiz scores counts for Module 3, so an optional attempt cannot lower your grade.

groups.name: 3.1 Effects of transactions on assets, liabilities and equity

qs.neutral_comments_html: Every event keeps Assets = Liabilities + Equity in balance. Buying on account or borrowing raises assets and liabilities; a credit sale or a share sale raises assets and equity; paying a supplier lowers assets and liabilities; paying an expense lowers assets and equity; swapping one asset for another changes nothing in total.
qs.question_text: Cullowhee pays $500 thousand in cash for wages earned by employees this month. Which effect on the accounting equation is correct? ($ thousand)

answers.answer_html: Assets no net change; liabilities no effect; equity no effect

groups.name: 3.13 Which events need a month-end adjustment

qs.neutral_comments_html: An adjustment is needed when an expense has been incurred (or revenue earned) but not yet recorded, or when a prepaid or deferred amount has been partly used. Cash events during the month are already recorded; an unrecorded accrued cost is not.
qs.question_text: Which one of these requires a month-end adjustment at Cullowhee?

answers.answer_html: Cullowhee has had its term loan outstanding all month and will pay the interest next month.
Cullowhee collected a dealer’s receivable on the 30th.
Cullowhee ordered parts that have not yet been delivered.

Enter numeric answers as plain numbers, with no $, commas or % sign. Your numbers are different from other students’ numbers.

groups.name: 4.3 What financial leverage does to ROE

qs.neutral_comments_html: ROE = ROA × financial leverage. If leverage stayed at 1.83, the whole change in ROE has to come from ROA, which fell because margin and turnover both fell.
qs.question_text: Cullowhee’s financial leverage was about 1.83 in both FY2025 and FY2026, but ROE fell from 16.0% to 10.4%. What does this tell you?

answers.answer_html: Leverage did not cause the decline. The fall came from ROA: a lower profit margin and slower asset turnover.
Nothing can be learned from leverage when ROE changes.
Higher leverage caused the decline in ROE.
Lower leverage caused the decline in ROE.

groups.name: 5.3 Why returns are estimated when the sale is recorded

qs.neutral_comments_html: Revenue recognition and expense recognition work together: the sale is recorded net of the returns and rebates the company expects, so net sales and profit match the period in which the sale was made.
qs.question_text: Why does Cullowhee estimate returns and dealer rebates when it records a sale, instead of waiting for the returns to arrive?

answers.answer_html: Accounting rules forbid recording a sale until the customer’s return period ends.
Revenue should be reported at the amount the company expects to keep, and the expense of returns belongs in the same period as the sale.
Returns are recorded only when cash is refunded, so the estimate reduces taxes.
Estimates let Cullowhee report higher gross sales.

qs.neutral_comments_html: The write-off reduces gross receivables and the allowance by the same amount, so net receivables do not change. The bad debt expense was recorded earlier, when the allowance was increased, so net income does not change at the write-off.
qs.question_text: Cullowhee writes off a specific dealer’s account as uncollectible, using the allowance method. What happens to net accounts receivable and to net income at that moment?

answers.answer_html: Net receivables decrease, but net income is unchanged.
Neither changes: the expense was already recorded when the allowance was set up.
Net income decreases, but net receivables are unchanged.
Net receivables and net income both decrease.

qs.question_text: A dealer returns a bike in January that Cullowhee sold in December. If Cullowhee already estimated returns when it recorded the December sale, what is the effect of the January return?

answers.answer_html: It reduces January’s net sales by the full price.
It increases the allowance for doubtful accounts.
The return uses up the existing estimate and does not reduce January’s sales again.

qs.neutral_comments_html: With rising costs, FIFO leaves the newest (highest) costs in ending inventory and charges the older (lower) costs to cost of goods sold. FIFO therefore has higher inventory, lower COGS and higher net income than LIFO.
qs.question_text: When battery pack costs are rising and inventory is not running out, which statement is true?

answers.answer_html: FIFO reports a higher ending inventory and a higher net income than LIFO.
LIFO reports a higher ending inventory and a higher net income than FIFO.
The two methods give the same net income if the company pays the same tax.
FIFO reports a higher cost of goods sold than LIFO.

groups.name: 6.9 Accounting for goodwill and acquired technology

qs.neutral_comments_html: Goodwill is an asset with an indefinite life. It is not amortized; it is tested for impairment, and an impairment loss is recorded if its carrying amount exceeds its value.
qs.question_text: After the acquisition of Highlands Cell Packs, how should Cullowhee account for the goodwill?

answers.answer_html: It is depreciated over the life of the equipment acquired.
It is not amortized. It is tested for impairment at least once a year and written down if its value has fallen.

The higher of your Gate Quiz and Mastery Quiz scores counts for Module 6, so an optional attempt cannot lower your grade.

groups.name: 6.9 Accounting for goodwill and acquired technology

qs.neutral_comments_html: Intangible assets with a limited life, like acquired technology, are amortized over their useful life (like depreciation). Goodwill is different because it has an indefinite life.
qs.question_text: Cullowhee’s acquired technology has an 8-year life. How is its cost reported?

answers.answer_html: It is expensed in the year of acquisition.
It is amortized over 8 years as an expense, reducing net income each year.
It is tested for impairment but never amortized.
